Q: When adding an element to a heap why don't we Heapify it from the root? A:

Adding a single element to a heap takes O(lg n) time. Applying the heap invariants to an unsorted array takes O(n lg n) time.

Critically, the "bubble up" step does not need to check the sibling nodes. Say you know subtree at the current node is a heap, so its root is its largest element. Assuming it has a parent, the parent is known to be larger then its other sibling (this is important); you are unclear whether the parent is larger than the current node. Then either

(1) The node is smaller than its parent, and the sibling is also smaller than its parent; the whole tree is a heap, stop.

(2) The node is larger than its parent, and therefore is also larger than the other sibling; so swap the values of the node and the parent, and repeat at the parent node if you're not at the root of the tree.

    5             5             5
   / \           / \           / \
  3   2  -->    3   2  -->   *4*  2
 /             / \           / \
1             1  *4*        1   3

For example: add 4 in the next position. The trivial subtree rooted at 4 is a heap. Compare with its parent (noting that 3 > 1); the node is greater than its parent, so swap. Compare again with its parent (noting that 5 < 4); the node is less than its parent, so the heap invariant holds everywhere.

This and your previous question are both about low-level details of heaps. IME it's unusual to use these directly. It's helpful to know that heaps exist, and for certain specific kinds of data access they can be useful. (In particular, if you're traversing a list in order but it's also being concurrently modified, a heap can give you the smallest item you haven't seen yet while still giving efficient O(lg n) traversal and updates.) More often you'll just use a heap as a means to get a priority queue.

In both cases, you'll usually just use a prebuilt library. In Python for example the standard library includes a heapq module with a heapq.heapify() function; you don't need to implement it yourself. (The documentation also describes some more use cases.)

I'd highly recommend finding a data-structures textbook or other introductory material for this class of question though. In the other question I had cited the Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, and Stein textbook which has in-depth discussions of the mechanics of heaps and other common data structures, including diagrams.

Q: Visual Studio 2019 can't load pdb files from microsoft symbol server. What to do? A:

Found the issue. The issue was that in the Symbol Caching path under Tools->Options->Debugger. I had given a path for which Visual Studio did not have the permission to write over there. Changed the path to a folder directly under C drive and it started working.

Q: How can I make this parallax effect work on mobile browsers? A:

That’s not true. Of course you can you just need to call the mobile css. Use it sparingly is a might become jumpy if you have a lot of images or a lot of content, and bogs it down.

CLASS mobile-parallax Add this class to any section, row, column, or module’s CSS classes box, set a background image, and turn on the parallax effect. Both true parallax and CSS parallax will work.

Q: How to add p values for correlation coefficients plotted using splom in lattice? A:

Another option is to use panel.text twice , with different adj parameter.

For example :

splom(~d.corr1, lower.panel = panel.splom,
      upper.panel = function(x, y, ...) {
      panel.fill(col = brewer.pal(9, "RdBu")[ round(cor(x, y) * 4 + 5)])
      cpl <- current.panel.limits()
      ## shift upward 
      panel.text(mean(cpl$xlim), mean(cpl$ylim),
                 round(cor(x, y),2), font=2, adj=c(0.5,-0.6))
      ## shift downward
      panel.text(mean(cpl$xlim), mean(cpl$ylim),
                 round( cor.test(x,y)$p.value, 2), font=1,
                 adj=c(0.5,0.6),col='blue')
      } )

Q: Can I use a :before or :after pseudo-element on an input field? A:

Modern browsers (since 2023) can use :has() from the parent element:

*:has(> .mystyle)::after { content:"😃"; }
<label><input class="mystyle" type="text" value="someValue"></label>

The content is added after the <input> but within its <label> container.

The OP noted a limitation:

Note: I cannot add a span around my input, because it is being generated by a third-party control.

There's still going to be a parent element, even if you can't control it. This should work as long as the text input is the only (or last) item in that container. It would be cleaner to better identify that containing element in your stylesheet, like label:has(> …)::after for this example.
